Lessons.Title: When and Why Do We Write Quadratic Equations?
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: translate a contextual target condition into a quadratic equation, compare rough graphical estimates with exact algebraic solutions, and decide which mathematical roots are contextually meaningful. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 2 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/2/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/2/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source revisits equations representing real constraints and asks when precise solving is necessary.

Original rectangle problem: a garden's length is five metres greater than its width x≥0 metres, with target area84m². Area equation x(x+5)=84, or x²+5x−84=0. Factoring gives (x+12)(x−7)=0 and algebraic candidates −12 and7; only x7 is a positive width, giving length12 and area84m².

Before exact solving, a graph of A(x)=x(x+5) suggests intersection with line y=84 near x7. Geometry requires nonnegative lengths, so the negative algebraic root is not physical. Distinguish writing equation (modeling) from solving it (finding admissible input). The factorization is an optional tool at this transition point and will be developed systematically later.

Student task: write an equation from area/perimeter language, estimate root on a labelled graph, independently verify width7, and critique a peer who accepts a negative side length. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for variable/domain, correct equation, checked root and interpretation of why one mathematical answer is invalid.

KeyConcepts.Title: Target equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Set function output equal to a specified contextual quantity.

KeyConcepts.Title: Quadratic constraint
KeyConcepts.Definition: Expanding a product of a variable with a related variable creates a squared term.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Bring terms to one side for comparison.

KeyConcepts.Title: Context root selection
KeyConcepts.Definition: An algebraic solution must also satisfy the variable's physical domain.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build target area equation
WorkedExamples.Question: Width x, length x+5, area84.
WorkedExamples.Method: Solve the original independently authored equation and check every candidate in the source expression.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find and check dimensions
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve x²+5x−84=0.
WorkedExamples.Method: Solve the original independently authored equation and check every candidate in the source expression.
Steps: Find factors with product−84 and sum+5:12 and−7.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both physically positive and exact area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish numerical and physical answers
WorkedExamples.Question: Why not x=−12?
WorkedExamples.Method: Solve the original independently authored equation and check every candidate in the source expression.
Steps: Substitute−12 into x(x+5): (−12)(−7)=84, so equation holds.
But a width of−12 metres is not a valid garden length.
Domain x≥0 is an independent constraint.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original area equality and domain both evaluated.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accepting every root as real-world quantity
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Negative lengths can make an algebraic product positive.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a graph intersection estimate as guaranteed exact
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A sketch resolution can conceal exact value.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use algebra and substitution to verify.

SummaryPoints: A contextual target often produces a quadratic equation.
Model construction and solving are distinct actions.
The area model has one admissible width7m and one invalid algebraic root−12.
Teacher evaluates equation choice and root interpretation.
